prompt.context:
The CEO of Zirgin Atlantic Airlines, Richard Branford, is considering starting a new direct airline route from London to Montreal. Zirgin currently runs flights in and out of both cities (as well as other cities globally) but not directly between the two cities. The company is currently at maximum capacity on their existing jets so any new route would require the use of a brand new airplane.

Zirgin Atlantic operates a flat pricing structure for its customers and would like to charge all passengers $500 for a round trip flight on this route ($250 for a one-way ticket). Zirgin Atlantic's strategy group has discovered that this pricing could likely draw an average of 200 round trip passengers every day.

Branford has approached us to recommend whether or not to open this new route. If we do decide to go forward with the route, he only wants to use one incremental airplane. Zirgin Atlantic is a subsidiary of Zirgin, a global conglomerate that also operates in the media and entertainment industry. As a benchmark, the company targets a 6-year payback period on its investments.
prompt.question: Should Zirgin Atlantic open the new direct London–Montreal route? Your analysis will cover: (1) purchase economics and payback period, (2) lease alternative economics, and (3) qualitative upsides and risks.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per year will the route be operational?
What are the variable costs per round trip flight?
What are the annual fixed costs (excluding the cost of the plane)?
What is the purchase price of a new plane?
What is the useful life of a new plane?
What is the annual lease cost if the company leases instead of buying?
clarifying_info.a: $10M per year, renewable at the same cost in perpetuity.

exhibits.title: Revenue Build
exhibits.shows: A table or structured layout presenting daily passenger volume, average ticket price, days operational per year, and the resulting daily and annual revenue figures for the proposed route.
exhibits.data: Daily passengers: 200 round trip (or 300 one-way); Avg ticket price: $500 round trip ($250 one-way); Days operational/year: 300; Daily revenue: $100,000; Annual revenue: $30M

exhibits.title: Cost Build and Payback Period
exhibits.shows: A table or structured layout presenting variable costs per round trip, annual fixed costs, the resulting total annual costs, capital investment for a new plane, and the payback period calculation.
exhibits.data: Variable cost per round trip: $40,000; Annual fixed costs (excl. plane): $3M; Annual variable costs: $12M; Total annual costs: $15M; Capital investment: $75M; Annual profit: $15M; Payback period: 5 years

framework: Part 1 – Purchase economics: Calculate annual revenue, annual costs, annual profit, and payback period; compare to the 6-year corporate benchmark.
Part 2 – Lease economics: Subtract annual lease cost from operating profit; assess profitability without upfront capital; compare buy vs. lease on total profit and risk profile.
Part 3 – Qualitative upside and downside: Identify strategic upsides (brand, synergies) and key risks (cannibalization, competition, industry risks).
Part 4 – Recommendation: Synthesize economics and qualitative factors into a concise recommendation with caveats.

questions.prompt: Part 1: If Zirgin purchases one new plane exclusively for this route, does the investment meet the company's 6-year payback target?
questions.guidance: Strong answer walks through revenue build (200 pax x $500 x 300 days = $30M/year), then costs (variable: $40k x 300 = $12M; fixed: $3M; total: $15M), arriving at annual profit of $15M. Then calculates payback = $75M / $15M = 5 years, which beats the 6-year target. Candidate should note the 25-year useful life means the route pays back the plane ~5x before replacement is needed.

math.setup: Annual revenue = 200 passengers x $500/pax x 300 days; Annual variable costs = $40,000/round trip x 300 days; Total annual costs = variable + fixed; Annual profit = revenue – costs; Payback period = capital investment / annual profit
math.answer: 5-year payback, which is below the 6-year corporate target — the investment meets criteria.

questions.prompt: Part 2: Richard Branford tells you the company can instead lease a plane for $10M/year in perpetuity. Is leasing economically profitable? How does it compare to buying?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate lease-scenario profit: $15M operating profit – $10M lease = $5M/year. Then compare buy vs. lease: buying generates $15M/year after 5-year payback ($375M total over 25 years) vs. leasing at $5M/year in perpetuity (lower annual profit but no upfront capital). Strong answer covers three risk dimensions: (1) asset base / balance sheet impact of buying, (2) exit flexibility — leasing is easier to exit if route fails, (3) opportunity cost of $75M capital deployed elsewhere.

math.setup: Annual profit under lease = operating profit – annual lease cost
steps: Buy total profit over 25 years = $15M x 25 = $375M (after 5-year payback, net = $375M – $75M = $300M)
Lease total profit over 25 years = $5M x 25 = $125M
math.answer: Leasing generates $5M/year profit — economically viable, but buying generates significantly more total profit ($300M net vs. $125M over 25 years). Trade-off is upfront capital and flexibility.

questions.prompt: Part 3: Aside from the pure economics, what are the potential upsides and risks of opening this new route?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure answer into upside catalysts and downside risks with brief rationale for each. A strong answer covers at least 2-3 points per side.

brainstorming.prompt: Aside from the pure economics of the route, what are some other potential upsides and risks to the plan?

categories.name: Potential Upsides
ideas: Brand exposure and marketing: A new direct route increases Zirgin brand visibility, especially in the Canadian market where Branford wants to grow presence.
Revenue synergies with existing routes: A new direct route creates new passenger transfer alternatives, potentially increasing demand on connecting routes.
Cost synergies with existing operations: The new route can share administrative and labor infrastructure with existing operations, lowering per-unit overhead.

categories.name: Potential Risks
ideas: Cannibalization: Zirgin already operates flights into and out of Montreal and London; a new direct route may steal customers who were previously making the same trip with stops or via nearby cities.
Competitive response: Opening the route signals entry into a new market and may invite aggressive pricing or capacity responses from existing carriers on the corridor.
General airline industry risks: Airlines are highly sensitive to consumer spending cycles, energy price volatility, and multinational regulatory/administrative complexity.

recommendation: The new London–Montreal route is financially attractive. Purchasing a new plane yields a 5-year payback — below the 6-year corporate target — and generates $15M/year in profit over a 25-year asset life.
If capital conservation or risk tolerance is a concern, leasing is also viable at $5M/year profit with no upfront investment, though total long-run returns are substantially lower.
My recommendation is to pursue the new route, with the buy option preferred on purely economic grounds, subject to review of competing capital uses.
risks: Cannibalization of existing Zirgin connecting-route passengers could reduce the net incremental demand below 200/day, eroding the economic case.
Energy price spikes or demand downturns could compress the $15M annual profit margin quickly given high fixed cost structure.
Buying a plane locks in $75M of capital and increases PP&E exposure; if the route fails, resale or redeployment of the asset may be costly.
next_steps: Validate the 200 round-trip passenger/day demand assumption with more detailed market research and competitive analysis of existing London–Montreal capacity.
Assess current capital deployment pipeline to determine whether the $75M purchase or lease structure is more aligned with overall portfolio priorities.
Model downside scenarios (e.g., 150 pax/day, fuel cost +20%) to stress-test the payback period before committing.
